why: Two sequences again: the elements you keep are a common subsequence, so insertions = len(finalList) - LCS. Because finalList has unique values, mapping each value to its index in finalList turns the O(n*m) LCS into a longest increasing subsequence.
hints: Whatever you do not insert must already appear in initialList in finalList's order. What is the largest such set?
Insertions = len(finalList) - LCS(finalList, initialList). With unique values in finalList, replace each initialList value by its index in finalList (drop values not present).
The LCS is then the longest strictly increasing subsequence of those indices: patience sorting with binary search, O(m log m).
pitfalls: Values of initialList that are not in finalList can never be matched; skip them.
Duplicates in initialList map to the same index; strict increase keeps them from counting twice.
statement:
You are given two integer lists finalList (length n, all values distinct) and initialList (length m, may contain duplicates).

In one operation you insert any integer at any position of initialList. Return the minimum number of insertions needed so that finalList becomes a subsequence of initialList (its values appear in initialList in the same order, not necessarily adjacent).

Example: finalList = [5, 1, 3], initialList = [9, 4, 2, 3, 4]. Only 3 of finalList already appears, so the longest part of finalList that already occurs in order has length 1. Insert 5 at the front and 1 before the 3: [5, 9, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4] contains 5, 1, 3 in order. The answer is 2.
constraints:
• 1 <= n, m <= 10^5
  • 1 <= finalList[i], initialList[j] <= 10^9
  • The values of finalList are distinct.
